Thank you, Mr. Krbenzoda, for the floor. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues. It is an honor and a pleasure to share some of the key findings of the report of the Secretary General on population, technology and research in the context of sustainable development. The report highlights that advances in technology and research have been instrumental in accelerating the implementation of the ICPD program of action and in strengthening its contribution to the sustainable development goals. At the same time, technological change has not benefited all populations equally. In some contexts, it has widened existing inequalities and created new divides. This makes it essential for countries to prioritize innovations that are inclusive, ethical, and grounded in human rights. It is crucial to invest in strengthening integrated population data systems. High quality, timely, and reliable population data are essential for tracking progress, identifying disparities, identifying those left furthest behind and hardest to reach, and guiding evidence-based policy making. To name just a couple of examples, innovations in information and communications technology have enhanced all phases of census operations, from mapping and enumeration to data processing and dissemination. Increasingly, countries are adopting multimodal population data systems that combine traditional censuses with civil registration and vital statistics, administrative data, geospatial tools, and real-time digital data sources. These integrated systems provide a more comprehensive and dynamic understanding of population trends. Countries can also leverage emerging technologies and advanced research to ensure healthy lives and promote well-being across all stages of the life course. In resource-constrained settings, prioritizing basic life-saving technologies and interventions remains essential. Expanding access to vaccines, improving maternal and newborn care, and scaling up simple, effective interventions to treat malnutrition and diarrheal diseases can save countless lives. Digital solutions, including e-health platforms and telemedicine, can further expand access to care, improve diagnosis and treatment, and empower people with the knowledge, tools, and resources they need to make informed decisions about their health and well-being. Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, big data analytics, and digital platforms also hold significant potential to strengthen forecasting, improve service delivery, and enhance monitoring and evaluation across health systems. Last but not least, it is also essential to strengthen national research capacity and foster local innovation ecosystems. This includes investing in universities and research institutions, supporting homegrown technological development, and advancing international cooperation so that innovations are grounded in local realities and capable of addressing diverse challenges. These innovations, when guided by rights-based approaches and ethical governance, can significantly advance the ICPD program of action and accelerate progress towards sustainable development.

Thank you.

It is also vital to invest in the development of safe digital tools that support age-appropriate, evidence-based programs to promote the health and well-being of adolescents and young people, including their mental health. Some examples of strategies in countries experiencing population aging Digital innovations can support healthy aging, promote independence, and strengthen long-term care systems. Innovations in assistive technologies, from mobility devices to smart home systems, can significantly enhance quality of life for older persons. These technological solutions must be designed with accessibility and usability at their core. Involving end users in the design and testing of digital tools ensures that technologies truly meet their needs. Robust data systems are also needed to monitor aging trends, assess care needs, and plan for the health and social care workforce. For countries facing rapid urbanization or significant migration flows, geospatial and mobility data can help governments plan urban services, transportation, and infrastructure more effectively. Digital solutions can promote the faster and cheaper transfer of migrant remittances, foster financial inclusion, enhance diaspora engagement and entrepreneurship, and improve access to information and relevant documentation for international migrants. In summary, tailoring technological and research approaches to demographic realities, whether characterized by youth, aging, mobility, or urbanization, ensures that innovations respond to actual population needs. In the 2020 census round, at least 39 countries moved to register based or combined census approaches, which integrate administrative records with survey data in ways that improve coverage and timeliness. Satellite imagery and geospatial tools have also been deployed to monitor refugee settlements in places like Bangladesh and track displacement in countries like South Sudan and Syria. Mobile phone data tracked displacement following the Haiti and Nepal earthquakes, as well as Cyclone Idai in Mozambique, offering near real-time insight that shaped humanitarian response. The lesson is the same across all these examples. Innovation works best when it strengthens, not replaces, foundational data systems such as censuses and civil registration and vital statistics. The translation of innovations is not complete until we talk about population responsive programs, which are equally encouraging to hear about. Ghana's mobile midwife service, for example, delivers maternal health support by mobile phone. Kenya's MTBA platform and South Africa's MomConnect connect women to prenatal care, and India's Sanjevini telemedicine platform has delivered over 150 consultations. On migration, mobile location data tracked return migration during COVID-19 lockdowns across many countries, including Indonesia, Nigeria, and many others. While M-Pesa mobile money records in Kenya and Uganda helped the UNHCR and UNFPA and partners refine service delivery to displaced populations. On urbanization, the UNFPA The United Nations Human Settlements Programme and the European Union Joint Research Centre have applied the new degree of urbanization methodology at the population grid level, producing harmonized urban and rural statistics that directly inform service delivery decisions. These are all building blocks. blocks of population intelligence, moving us from statistics to targeted action. And solutions must also reflect our demographic diversity, which was the second part of my question. So rather than applying just single technological templates, in many countries, there have been examples of how this has been translated into service delivery. In high fertility settings, we also have self-injecting contraception and self-sampling HPV kits that are reaching women in humanitarian settings. No single approach, I can say, serves all contexts, but the ambition is to move from data to population intelligence. Without data, we can't target and we can't have impact. What then needs to change? Let me highlight three things that came out of the report. That first, we have to treat data as infrastructure. Population data systems such as censuses, civil registration, admin systems are not optional. They are essential just as health systems, education systems need to be sustained. They also need to have predictable financing. So data is infrastructure, it's not a project. Second, we need to move beyond reliance on official development assistance. With declining aid, countries need to strengthen domestic financing and integrate data into national development plans. Third, we need to invest in research and capacity. Many countries in sub-Saharan Africa, for example, invest less than 0.4% of GDP in research and development, compared to 2.6% in high-income countries. The region also has fewer than 100 researchers per million people, compared to over 4,000 in high-income countries. So the goal must be to move from data to population intelligence, where every country has the tools and the human capital to translate evidence into action. Dear Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, we cannot solve the problems of today and tomorrow with the tools of yesterday. In today's world, digitalization, e-health and AI are rapidly transforming health care. The AI revolution is expected to be not only 10 times faster, but also 10 times more impactful than the Industrial Revolution, which is precisely why we must actively engage with technology to ensure sustainable development and build resilient, healthy societies. However, this transformation is not a sprint, it's rather a marathon. And to move forward responsibly, we must first compartmentalize the hype around AI and focus on its real foundations. AI is built on data, but data relies on trust. Without the trust of individuals providing often highly sensitive health information, data sharing remains limited. And without sufficient data, these systems cannot reach their full potential. Secondly, we must recognize that technological progress is not equally distributed. While around 1 billion people are using AI today, the global population exceeds 8 billion. which highlights the risk of deepening inequalities in an already fragmented world. And these gaps are not only between countries and populations, but also within them. From a medical perspective, I have observed that access to technology does not always transfer into access to care. In clinical settings, I have encountered patients who were formally included in digital health systems, yet were unable to benefit from them due to barriers in usability, access, or design. This raises a fundamental equity concern for vulnerable populations, particularly people with limited resources or older adults, precisely the groups that are growing in size due to global demographic aging trends. Therefore, technology alone is not enough. We need reliable data, but also usability, digital literacy, and inclusive design. At the same time, technology holds significant potential to improve health care delivery, especially in rural and underserved areas, from logistics and resource distribution to early screening and prevention. Often it is not large scale solutions, but single strategic steps that can have the greatest impact. Ultimately, the impact of technology will not be determined by innovation alone, but by how we ensure it truly works for everyone.

Chair, distinguished delegates. In 1994, the Programme of Action of the ICPD established that quality data are the indispensable condition for evidence-based policymaking. Delegates, Excellencies, it is an honor to address the Commission on Population and Development during its 59th session. We meet at the time when profound demographic, technological and social transformations reshape our societies and when the commitments of the ICPD Programme of Action remain more relevant than ever. The reports of the Secretary General highlight both promises and risks of technological change and advancing sustainable development. The Government Population Council's assessments of Poland's demographic situation illustrate how these global megatrends manifest at a national level. Allow me to share several reflections. First, our discussions confirm that the high quality population data are the foundation of effective policy. Both Secretary General's reports underline the urgency of building interoperable, secure and human rights-based data ecosystems that integrate censuses, registers, surveys and geospatial sources. Poland's national assessments shows how critical these investments are. We face significant demographic shifts, a record low fertility rate, continuing natural population decline, accelerated aging and increasing migration flows. Addressing these challenges requires reliable, timely and harmonized data, including improvements in vital statistics, access to administrative microdata and long-term panel surveys, along with adequate privacy protection. We strongly support the recommendation to strengthen national capacities for population statistics and digital governance. Second, demographic trends across the world and in Poland reveal the urgency of investing in sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights. The global report demonstrates how new technologies from AI-assisted diagnostics to telemedicine can expand access and reduce inequalities. Poland's experience confirms that people's capabilities to realize their reproductive intentions depend not only on access to medical services and knowledge about fertility care, but also on social norms, gender equality, and balance between family and work. Despite widespread desire to have children, persistently low fertility, a rise in one-child preferences and increasing childlessness reflect unmet needs for support throughout the life course. We echo the Secretary-General's call to expand research, ensure ethical governance of emerging reproductive technologies, and strengthen the accessibility, affordability, and quality of reproductive health care services. Third, the rapid aging of populations demands integrated policy responses. In Poland, the share of people aged 65 plus is approaching 20% and rising rapidly. This mirrors a global trend that requires substantial investments in long-term care, assistive technologies, healthy aging strategies, and labor market adaptation. Digital health, telemedicine, and general technology can significantly improve autonomy and quality of life of older persons, but only if designed inclusively and governed responsibly. We also note the growing role of automation and robotics in care systems for aging populations, crucial for both caregivers and care receivers. We strongly support recommendations to expand access to assistive technologies and embed equity, safety, and universal design in all technological solutions. Fourth, the Secretary-General's reports rightly emphasize that technology can both deepen and bridge inequalities. In Poland, internal and international migrations have become key elements of shaping local labour markets, education systems and social cohesion. Digital tools improve access to services for migrants, strengthen administrative coordination and facilitate inclusion. At the same time, we must protect privacy and prevent a discriminatory use of digital identity and surveillance tools. Likewise, we must ensure that digitalization reduces rather than exacerbates gender inequality. Technology facilitates gender-based violence, misinformation, and unsafe online spaces, and threatens the rights, dignity, and participation of women, youth, and older persons. We support the Global Digital Compact call for rights-based regulation, safety by design approaches, and universal digital literacy. Finally, both global and national analysis underscore the need to integrate demographic considerations into economic and social policy. Declining fertility, aging, regional disparities, and changing household structures require comprehensive forward-looking strategies. For Poland, this includes expanding childcare and eldercare infrastructure, improving work-life balance, creating conditions that enable people to realize their family plans, investing in lifelong learning, and harnessing the contributions of migrants. For all countries, this means aligning technology and demographic policy to promote human development, gender equality, and resilience. Chair, the challenges that we face are complex, but the evidence is clear. Technology can be a powerful source for equitable development if guided by human rights, inclusiveness and solidarity. Demographic change must not be viewed as a burden and threat for development and people's well-being, but as a call to redesign systems, institutions and policies for sustainable future. We thank the Secretary-General for his comprehensive report. And we reaffirm our commitment to the ICPD Programme of Action, to the Digital Global Compact, and to strengthening international cooperation so that no individual, regardless of...

Act.
